Ohm's Law and Power

Unit 3: Electricity and Electronics. Lesson 11 of 53 in BMET Academy.

One equation ties the three quantities together, and a second one tells you how much heat the circuit makes. Between them they answer most of the numeric questions on the exam and explain why electricity is dangerous.

Ohm's law

V = I x R        volts  = amps x ohms
I = V / R        amps   = volts / ohms
R = V / I        ohms   = volts / amps

The triangle trick: write V on top with I and R side by side underneath. Cover the one you want and the other two show you the operation. V over something means divide; two values side by side means multiply.

Worked example: 12 V across 4 ohm. Cover I, and you are left with V over R: 12 / 4 = 3 A.

Power

Power is the rate at which electrical energy turns into heat, light, or motion. It is measured in watts.

P = V x I            the one to reach for first
P = I squared x R    when you know current and resistance
P = V squared / R    when you know voltage and resistance

Same example: 12 V at 3 A is 12 x 3 = 36 W.

Power ratings matter because every resistor is also a small heater. A common hobby resistor is rated a quarter watt. Ask it for more and it discolors, drifts, and eventually opens. In your lab, 9 V across 470 ohm draws about 19 mA and dissipates about 0.17 W, comfortably under the rating. Drop the resistor to 47 ohm and the same battery asks for 1.7 W, seven times the rating, and the part cooks.

Why Ohm's law is the safety lesson

Current is what injures people, and Ohm's law says what sets the current: the voltage available and the resistance in the path. The voltage of an outlet is fixed at 120 V. The variable is you.

Dry, intact skin     about 100,000 ohm    120 V / 100,000 = about 1 mA   a tingle
Wet or broken skin   about 1,000 ohm      120 V / 1,000  = 120 mA        likely fatal

Nothing about the outlet changed. Sweat, a spilled bag of saline, a cut on your thumb, or a gel-covered electrode changed the denominator, and the current went up a hundredfold. That is the entire argument for dry hands, intact gloves, and keeping liquids off the bench.

A circuit worked end to end

A 9 V battery and one 470 ohm resistor in a loop:

  1. Current: I = V / R = 9 / 470 = 0.019 A, which is 19 mA.
  2. Power in the resistor: P = V x I = 9 x 0.019 = 0.17 W.
  3. Check it the other way: P = V squared / R = 81 / 470 = 0.17 W. The two agree, so the arithmetic is sound.

In the lab you measure the voltage and the current on that exact circuit, then compute R and P from your own readings instead of trusting the color bands. When a measured R lands within a few percent of the printed value, you have proved both the law and your technique.

Exam tip: convert to plain amps, volts, and ohms before you divide. 470 ohm and 19 mA is 0.019 A, not 19, and that one slip turns 470 ohm into 0.47 ohm.
Remember
V = I x R, I = V / R, R = V / I; P = V x I, P = I squared x R, P = V squared / R. 12 V across 4 ohm is 3 A and 36 W. Quarter-watt resistors cook if asked for more. Body resistance about 100,000 ohm dry gives about 1 mA from 120 V; about 1,000 ohm wet gives 120 mA. Convert mA to amps before dividing.

Deeper explanation

Ohm's Law and Power, explained slowly

The triangle, and why it works

         V
      -------
      I  |  R

cover V  ->  V = I x R
cover I  ->  I = V / R
cover R  ->  R = V / I

The three forms are one relationship read three ways: the current through a resistance is proportional to the voltage across it. Double the push and you double the flow. Double the opposition and you halve the flow.

Worked examples to copy

Known                    Find        Work                     Answer
12 V across 4 ohm        current     12 / 4                   3 A
0.5 A through 100 ohm    voltage     0.5 x 100                50 V
9 V and 19 mA measured   resistance  9 / 0.019                about 474 ohm
120 V across 1,000 ohm   current     120 / 1000               0.12 A = 120 mA
24 V, need 10 mA         resistance  24 / 0.010               2,400 ohm

The third row is the lab. You measure the voltage and the current and compute a resistance you never measured, then compare it with the color bands. When they agree you have proved your technique as well as the law.

Power: the other equation

P = V x I            volts x amps
P = I squared x R    when current and resistance are known
P = V squared / R    when voltage and resistance are known

12 V at 3 A         = 36 W
0.019 A in 470 ohm  = 0.019 x 0.019 x 470 = 0.17 W
9 V across 470 ohm  = 81 / 470 = 0.17 W

The last two rows are the same circuit computed two ways, which is a free check on your arithmetic: if two routes disagree, one of them used a wrong number.

Power matters because it is heat. A resistor is rated for the heat it can shed, commonly a quarter watt on a hobby part and one or more watts on power resistors. Asking a quarter-watt part for 1.7 W does not blow it instantly; it discolors, its value drifts, the device develops an intermittent fault, and weeks later it opens. Burnt or discolored resistors on a board are a message: either the part was underrated or something else failed and overloaded it. Replacing it without finding out which is how you get the same board back.

The shock arithmetic

Ohm's law is the reason electrical safety numbers are what they are. The outlet's 120 V is fixed; the path resistance is not.

Path                           Resistance         Current from 120 V   Effect
dry hand to dry hand           about 100,000 ohm  about 1.2 mA         perception, a tingle
sweaty hands, metal tools      about 10,000 ohm   12 mA                past let-go: cannot release
wet skin, standing in water    about 1,000 ohm    120 mA               fibrillation likely

Nothing about the electricity changed in those three rows. Your skin did. That is the argument for dry hands, intact insulation on your tools, no rings or watches at the bench, keeping fluid away from powered equipment, and never making yourself the second connection to ground.

The same arithmetic in reverse explains microshock: a current as small as 10 microamps delivered directly to the heart through a catheter or a pacing lead can cause fibrillation, because the skin's resistance is not in the path at all. Microamps outside the body are nothing; microamps inside it are the reason leakage limits exist.

Convert before you divide. Every wrong answer on this material comes from leaving a value in milliamps or kilohms.
